meta.title: Hausa A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hausa → English (see the Hausa, recall the meaning) and English → Hausa (see an English meaning, recall the Hausa). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hausa, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 294 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, the days of the week, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and particles every sentence is built out of — and the other 206 are the commonest remaining words in the Tatoeba collection of Hausa sentences, counted by the WHOLE word (a noun's plural and its forms with the linker and the possessive endings added together). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed as Hausa is ordinarily written, in the Latin alphabet with its hooked letters (ɓ ɗ ƙ and 'y); beneath it, where English Wiktionary gives one, is the same word with its TONES and VOWEL LENGTH marked, which ordinary writing leaves out: a high tone is unmarked, a low tone takes a grave accent (à), a falling tone a circumflex (â), and a long vowel a macron (ā) — ruwā 'water', màcḕ 'woman'. 362 of the 500 words have that line. 137 of the 500 are glossed by Folio itself rather than taken from Wiktionary, which lacks some of the commonest words in the language (yi 'to do', tafi 'to go', da 'and, with'); those carry no tone line, since a tone that no source states is not printed. The nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, and their plural, which in Hausa is seldom predictable, wherever the source gives them. Real example sentences come with 495 of the 500 words, three apiece for 493 of them, with the word picked out in colour; the sentences are as Tatoeba's contributors wrote them, which is not always with the hooks. There is no read-aloud button: few devices carry a Hausa voice, and one without it reads the word in English. The Hausa Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the hooked letters and the other sounds English spelling has no letter for. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, tone, gender and plurals: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0), and Folio's own glosses for the words it lacks. Frequency and example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
